title: How NOT to benchmark your SITE metric: Beyond Static Leaderboards and Towards Realistic Evaluation.
topic: General Machine Learning->Transfer, Multitask and Meta-learning
claim: A model-selection metric takes a pool of candidate models and a target dataset, extracts features, and scores each model to produce a ranking.
layout: 3 columns, left-to-right: boxed model zoo, central feature extraction and estimation stages with target dataset feeding in from above, boxed ranked models with scores on the right; math labels on arrows
description: A left-to-right flow diagram. On the left, a rounded purple box labeled "Model Zoo" holds three hand-drawn neural-network sketches in green, blue and pink. In the center, a "Target Dataset" mosaic of small photos (flowers, cars, textures, aerial imagery) sits on top. An arrow labeled x leads from the images down to a "Feature Extraction" (φ) stage. A second arrow labeled "Labels y" runs to a "Transferability Estimation" stage with the formula T_m(φ(x), y). Black arrows connect the stages from the model zoo to the right. On the right, a second purple box labeled "Ranked Models" stacks the same three networks, ordered Φ3 (score 1.0), Φ2 (0.7) and Φ1 (0.5). The colored networks catch the eye first, and the central pipeline follows.
caption: Illustration of Source Independent Transferability Estimation (SITE): Given a set of pre-trained models (on the left), a SITE metric computes a score $T_m$ based on extracted features on a target dataset. The scores $T_m$ are used to rank the pre-trained models according to their transferability.
abstract: Transferability estimation metrics are used to find a high-performing pre-trained model for a given target task without fine-tuning models and without access to the source dataset. Despite the growing interest in developing such metrics, the benchmarks used to measure their progress have gone largely unexamined. In this work, we empirically show the shortcomings of widely used benchmark setups to evaluate transferability estimation metrics. We argue that the benchmarks on which these metrics are evaluated are fundamentally flawed. We empirically demonstrate that their unrealistic model spaces and static performance hierarchies artificially inflate the perceived performance of existing metrics, to the point where simple, dataset-agnostic heuristics can outperform sophisticated methods. Our analysis reveals a critical disconnect between current evaluation protocols and the complexities of real-world model selection. To address this, we provide concrete recommendations for constructing more robust and realistic benchmarks to guide future research in a more meaningful direction.
